chunks: Why the supply goes close to the load. The question: Why do you want to place your power supply close to the load?
Every millimeter of wire between a supply and its load is a small resistor and a small inductor in series. The resistor wastes voltage while current flows steadily.
The inductor makes the voltage dip when the current changes fast. The regulator also cannot see these losses, because it measures its own output, not the load.
So you place the supply and its output capacitors as close to the load as heat and noise allow.
Imagine a water tower feeding a house through a very long, narrow pipe. Even with the tower full, the house gets low pressure because of friction in the pipe.
And if you open every tap at once, the pipe's inertia makes the pressure collapse for a moment before the flow catches up.
The tower's gauge reads fine the whole time, because it is at the tower, not the house.
The regulator is an ideal source on the left; R p and L p stand for the supply and return wiring (the return is lumped into the top rail for clarity).
The local capacitor C loc supplies fast load steps. The load voltage is what remains after R p , L p and any capacitor droop.
IR drop: the voltage I times R lost in the supply and return wiring ("High-current layout rules of thumb"). Droop: a brief dip in the load voltage during a current step.
L di over dt : the voltage across an inductance when the current changes quickly ("Long vs short power traces and shapes").
Remote sense: extra wires that let the regulator measure the voltage at the load.
Local decoupling: capacitors at the load pins that supply fast transients ("Routing decoupling and bulk capacitors").
A 1 volts rail feeds a 10 amps load. The supply and return are each 20 mm of 1 mm wide, 1 oz copper, so 20 squares at 0. 48 milliohms is 9. 6 milliohms each. Together that is 19.
2 milliohms, and the drop is 10 times 0. 0192 equals 0. 19 volts, about a fifth of the rail. Now add 10 nanohenries of trace inductance and a 5 amps step in 100 nanoseconds.
The dip is 10 nanohenries times 5 amps over 100 nanoseconds equals 0. 5 volts. That is the whole idea.
"Distance adds resistance and inductance to the supply path.
At 1 volts and 10 amps, 20 mm of 1 mm trace each way drops about 190 millivolts, and 10 nanohenries with a 5 amps step in 100 nanoseconds droops half a volt.
The regulator can't compensate, because its feedback senses its own output, not the load, and the extra inductance hurts the loop. Long traces also radiate and pick up noise.
So I place the regulator and output capacitors next to the load, or use remote sense and a point-of-load regulator."
